title: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: A.4 Rigid body mechanics — IB Diploma Programme Physics (guide first assessment 2025, updated November 2023), topic A.4.
meta_desc: IB DP Physics practice covering A.4 Rigid body mechanics, guide topic A.4.
final_note: You worked through A.4 Rigid body mechanics — 12 guide statements.

concepts.def: The turning effect of a force about an axis, τ = Fr sin θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, r is the distance from the axis to the point where the force is applied, and θ is the angle between the line of action of the force and the line from the axis to that point. SI unit: N m. The torque is greatest when the force acts at right angles to that line (θ = 90°) and zero when its line of action passes through the axis (θ = 0° or 180°).

concepts.term: Perpendicular distance of the line of action
concepts.def: The quantity r sin θ in τ = Fr sin θ: the shortest distance from the axis to the line of action of the force. The torque equals the force multiplied by this perpendicular distance, so moving the point of application along the line of action does not change the torque.

Whether a torque tends to turn a body clockwise or counter-clockwise about the axis, as seen from one chosen side. Torques in opposite senses are given opposite signs when they are combined, so a resultant torque is found by subtracting the total torque in one sense from the total in the other. The vector nature of torque is not required.

The state of a body whose resultant torque is zero, so it has no angular acceleration: it is either not rotating or rotating at a constant angular speed. For a body at rest the total clockwise torque about any axis equals the total counter-clockwise torque about the same axis. Rotational equilibrium is independent of translational equilibrium (zero resultant force); a body in full equilibrium needs both.

The point of an extended body at which, for linear motion, its whole mass may be taken as concentrated; the weight of the body can be taken to act there. For a uniform symmetrical body such as a uniform plank it is at the geometric centre. It does not replace the mass distribution when rotation is considered: the moment of inertia depends on where all the mass is. Calculating the position of the centre of mass is not required.

An extended body whose shape and size do not change when forces act on it, so the distance between any two of its particles is fixed. Every particle of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis turns through the same angle in the same time, so the whole body has one angular displacement, one angular velocity and one angular acceleration.

A non-zero sum of the torques acting on a body about an axis, with torques of opposite sense subtracted. An unbalanced torque on an extended rigid body causes angular acceleration, just as an unbalanced force causes linear acceleration. A body can experience an unbalanced torque when the resultant force on it is zero, for example two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide.

concepts.term: Angular position and angular displacement (θ, Δθ)
concepts.def: Angular position θ is the angle of a line fixed in the body measured from a reference direction; angular displacement Δθ is the change in angular position. Both are measured in radians (rad): one revolution is 2π rad, and an arc of length s at radius r subtends Δθ = s/r.

The rate of change of angular position, ω = Δθ/Δt; its magnitude is the angular speed. SI unit: rad s⁻¹. All points of a rigid body share the same ω, while the linear speed of a point at distance r from the axis is v = ωr. A body making f revolutions per second has ω = 2πf. A formal vector treatment is not required.
The rate of change of angular velocity, α = Δω/Δt. SI unit: rad s⁻². It is caused by an unbalanced torque, and is zero whenever the body rotates at a constant angular speed.

Motion of a round body along a surface in which the point in contact with the surface is instantaneously at rest, so the speed of the centre of mass v and the angular speed ω about the centre are linked by v = ωR, where R is the radius. It is the only combination of rotational and translational motion considered in the course.

For constant α: Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ. They are the rotational counterparts of the equations for uniform linear acceleration, with Δθ, ω and α replacing s, v and a. Angles must be in radians and a slowing body has α of opposite sign to ω.

The property of a body that measures its resistance to angular acceleration about a particular axis, playing the role in rotation that mass plays in linear motion. SI unit: kg m². It depends on the mass of the body and on how that mass is distributed about the axis: mass further from the axis contributes more. The same body has different moments of inertia about different axes. Formulas for specific mass distributions are provided when needed.

concepts.term: Moment of inertia of a system of point masses
concepts.def: I = Σmr², the sum over all the masses of each mass multiplied by the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis. Because r is squared, doubling the distance of a mass from the axis quadruples its contribution, while a mass on the axis contributes nothing.

τ = Iα, where τ is the average resultant torque on a body about an axis, I is its moment of inertia about that axis and α its angular acceleration. For the same resultant torque, a body with a larger moment of inertia has a smaller angular acceleration.

For an extended body rotating about an axis, L = Iω. SI unit: kg m² s⁻¹ (equivalent to N m s). It depends on both the moment of inertia (so on the mass distribution) and the angular speed. The vector nature of angular momentum is not required.

The angular momentum of a body or system stays constant unless a resultant external torque acts on it. When the moment of inertia of an extended body changes (a skater pulling in her arms) or two bodies become coupled (a disc dropped onto a rotating turntable), Iω before equals Iω after, so the angular speed changes. Kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved in these processes.

The product of the average resultant torque and the time for which it acts, ΔL = τΔt, equal to the change in angular momentum Δ(Iω). SI unit: N m s (equivalent to kg m² s⁻¹). On a torque–time graph it is the area under the graph. Torques of opposite sense produce angular impulses of opposite sign.

The kinetic energy of a body due to its rotation, E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I. SI unit: J. For a fixed angular momentum, the rotational kinetic energy is inversely proportional to the moment of inertia, so a body that reduces its moment of inertia while L stays constant gains rotational kinetic energy from work done by internal forces.

concepts.term: Kinetic energy of a rolling body
concepts.def: A body rolling without slipping has translational kinetic energy ½Mv² (its mass treated as concentrated at the centre of mass, moving at v) and rotational kinetic energy ½Iω² about the centre of mass, with ω = v/R. The total is ½Mv² + ½Iω². On a slope, the larger the fraction of energy that goes into rotation, the smaller the speed gained for a given loss of gravitational potential energy.

mcqs.q: A mechanic tightens a nut with a spanner. She applies a force of 45 N to the handle at a point 0.30 m from the axis of the nut. The force makes an angle of 70° with the line joining the axis to the point where the force is applied. What is the magnitude of the torque of this force about the axis?
mcqs.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
mcqs.explain: τ = Fr sin θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the line from the axis to the point of application: τ = 45 × 0.30 × sin 70° = 13.5 × 0.940 = 12.7 N m.
rationales: A student who uses cos θ, as in the equation for work, gets 45 × 0.30 × cos 70° = 4.62 N m. The turning component of the force is the one perpendicular to the line from the axis, F sin θ.
τ = Fr sin θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the line from the axis to the point of application: τ = 45 × 0.30 × sin 70° = 13.5 × 0.940 = 12.7 N m.
A student who multiplies force by distance and ignores the angle gets 45 × 0.30 = 13.5 N m. That is the torque only when the force is at 90° to the line from the axis; at 70° it is smaller.
A student whose calculator is in radian mode gets sin 70 = 0.774 and 13.5 × 0.774 = 10.4 N m. The angle is in degrees; sin 70° = 0.940.

mcqs.q: A rigid body is free to turn about a fixed axis. One of the forces acting on it lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis. Under which condition is the torque of this force about the axis zero?
options: It acts perpendicular to the line from the axis to where it acts.
The body remains at rest while this force acts on it.
An equal force acts on the other side, at the same distance.
Its line of action passes through the axis of rotation.
mcqs.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
mcqs.explain: τ = Fr sin θ. If the line of action passes through the axis, θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0; equivalently the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action is zero.
rationales: A student who uses cos θ in the torque equation thinks a perpendicular force gives zero torque. In fact θ = 90° gives sin θ = 1, the maximum torque for that force and distance.

A student who thinks a torque exists only when the body turns picks this. A body can stay at rest while this force exerts a torque, if other torques balance it; the force's own torque is still Fr sin θ.

A student who thinks a balancing force removes this force's own torque picks this. An equal force on the other side at the same distance can make the RESULTANT torque zero, but the torque of this force is still Fr sin θ, which other forces do not change.
τ = Fr sin θ. If the line of action passes through the axis, θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0; equivalently the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action is zero.

mcqs.q: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 150 N rests on a pivot 1.2 m from end A. A load of weight 90 N hangs from the other end, B. The weight of the plank acts at its midpoint. What weight must hang from end A for the plank to rest horizontally in equilibrium?
mcqs.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
mcqs.explain: Take torques about the pivot. The plank's weight acts 0.80 m from the pivot on the B side and the load at B is 2.8 m from it: 150 × 0.80 + 90 × 2.8 = 372 N m in one sense. W × 1.2 = 372, so W = 310 N.
mcqs.working: Take torques about the pivot (the pivot force then has no torque). Midpoint is 2.0 m from A, i.e. 0.80 m from the pivot on the B side; B is 2.8 m from the pivot. Torque in the B sense: (150 N)(0.80 m) + (90 N)(2.8 m) = 120 + 252 = 372 N m. Torque in the A sense: W(1.2 m). Rotational equilibrium: 1.2W = 372, so W = 310 N.
rationales: Take torques about the pivot. The plank's weight acts 0.80 m from the pivot on the B side and the load at B is 2.8 m from it: 150 × 0.80 + 90 × 2.8 = 372 N m in one sense. W × 1.2 = 372, so W = 310 N.

A student who ignores the plank's own weight gets W × 1.2 = 90 × 2.8, so W = 210 N. The plank's weight acts at its midpoint, 0.80 m from the pivot, and has a torque of 120 N m that must also be balanced.

A student who balances forces rather than torques makes the weight at A equal to 150 + 90 = 240 N. Equilibrium needs the torques about the pivot to balance, and each force's distance from the pivot matters.

A student who uses positions measured from end A as the distances takes 2.0 m for the plank's weight and 4.0 m for the load at B: 1.2W = 150 × 2.0 + 90 × 4.0 = 660 N m, so W = 550 N. Distances must be measured from the pivot: 0.80 m for the plank's weight and 2.8 m for the load.

mcqs.q: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium. Which statement about the body must be true?
options: The body is not rotating about any axis.
The forces on each side of its axis are equal.
The resultant torque acting on the body is zero.
The resultant force acting on the body is zero.
mcqs.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
mcqs.explain: Rotational equilibrium is defined by zero resultant torque, so there is no angular acceleration. The body may be at rest or rotating at a constant angular speed.
rationales: A student who equates equilibrium with being at rest picks this. A body with zero resultant torque has constant angular velocity, which need not be zero: a wheel spinning steadily on a frictionless axle is in rotational equilibrium.
A student who judges balance by equal forces picks this. The torques must balance, and a small force far from the axis can balance a large force close to it.
Rotational equilibrium is defined by zero resultant torque, so there is no angular acceleration. The body may be at rest or rotating at a constant angular speed.

A student who merges the two equilibrium conditions picks this. Zero resultant torque does not require zero resultant force: a box pulled along by a force through its centre of mass accelerates without rotating.

mcqs.q: A uniform bar lies at rest on frictionless horizontal ice. Two horizontal forces of equal, constant magnitude are then applied, one at each end of the bar, in opposite directions; each force is kept perpendicular to the bar at all times. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the bar while the forces act is correct?
options: It stays at rest and does not turn.
It rotates at a constant angular speed.
mcqs.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
mcqs.explain: The forces act along different lines and turn the bar in the same sense, so the resultant torque is not zero; it stays constant because each force stays perpendicular to the bar, so the angular acceleration α = τ/I is constant and the angular speed increases steadily. The forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero and the centre of mass stays at rest.
rationales: A student who treats zero resultant force as full equilibrium picks this. Zero resultant force keeps the centre of mass at rest, but the two forces act along different lines and turn the bar in the same sense, so there is a resultant torque and the bar gains angular speed.

The forces act along different lines and turn the bar in the same sense, so the resultant torque is not zero; it stays constant because each force stays perpendicular to the bar, so the angular acceleration α = τ/I is constant and the angular speed increases steadily. The forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero and the centre of mass stays at rest.

A student who thinks a steady torque keeps a body turning at a steady rate picks this. A constant resultant torque gives a constant angular acceleration (α = τ/I), so the angular speed keeps increasing for as long as the forces act.

A student who thinks off-centre forces move a body as well as turn it picks this. The motion of the centre of mass depends only on the resultant force, a_cm = F/M, and here the equal and opposite forces give F = 0, so the centre of mass stays at rest; the forces only make the bar turn.

mcqs.q: A wheel is mounted on a frictionless axle. Starting from rest, a constant resultant torque acts on it for a few seconds and is then removed. How does the wheel move after the torque is removed?
options: It keeps rotating at a constant angular speed.
It slows down steadily and then stops rotating.
Its angular speed rises until the torque is used up.
It stops, as its angular acceleration is now zero.
mcqs.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
mcqs.explain: With no resultant torque there is no angular acceleration (α = τ/I = 0), so the wheel keeps the angular speed it had when the torque was removed. This is the rotational form of Newton's first law.
rationales: With no resultant torque there is no angular acceleration (α = τ/I = 0), so the wheel keeps the angular speed it had when the torque was removed. This is the rotational form of Newton's first law.
A student who thinks a torque is needed to keep a body rotating picks this. Real wheels slow because friction exerts a torque; on a frictionless axle nothing changes the angular speed.
A student who pictures the torque as stored in the wheel picks this. Angular acceleration exists only while a torque acts: once the torque is removed, α = 0 at once.
A student who confuses zero angular acceleration with zero angular velocity picks this. α = 0 means the angular velocity is constant, at the non-zero value reached when the torque stopped.

mcqs.q: A bicycle travels along a level road at a constant 7.0 m s⁻¹. Its wheels, each of diameter 0.70 m, roll without slipping. What is the angular speed of each wheel?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
mcqs.explain: For rolling without slipping v = ωr, with r = 0.70/2 = 0.35 m. ω = v/r = 7.0/0.35 = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: Rolling without slipping: v = ωr, r = 0.70 m/2 = 0.35 m. ω = v/r = (7.0 m s⁻¹)/(0.35 m) = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who uses the diameter as the radius gets 7.0/0.70 = 10.0 rad s⁻¹. The distance from the axle to the rim is the radius, 0.35 m.
A student who divides by the circumference gets 7.0/(2π × 0.35) = 3.18. That is the number of revolutions per second, not the angular speed in rad s⁻¹; multiply by 2π to get 20.0 rad s⁻¹.
A student who treats linear and angular speed as the same quantity gives 7.00 rad s⁻¹. They are linked by v = ωr, so ω = v/r = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.
For rolling without slipping v = ωr, with r = 0.70/2 = 0.35 m. ω = v/r = 7.0/0.35 = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: A rigid disc rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axis through its centre. Point P on the disc is 0.10 m from the axis and point Q is 0.20 m from the axis. How do the motions of P and Q compare?
options: Q has twice the angular velocity and twice the linear speed.
Both have the same angular velocity and the same linear speed.
Same angular velocity; Q has twice the linear speed of P.
Q has half the angular velocity of P, because ω = v/r.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
mcqs.explain: Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time, so P and Q share one angular velocity. Linear speed v = ωr, so Q, at twice the distance, has twice the linear speed.
rationales: A student who does not separate angular from linear speed thinks the faster-moving point Q must also rotate faster. Both points complete a revolution in the same time, so their angular velocities are equal.
A student who thinks every part of a rigid body moves at the same speed picks this. In rotation Q travels round a circle twice as large in the same time, so its linear speed v = ωr is twice P's.
Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time, so P and Q share one angular velocity. Linear speed v = ωr, so Q, at twice the distance, has twice the linear speed.
A student who reads ω = v/r with v held constant picks this. On a rigid body ω is the same everywhere; it is v that is proportional to r.

mcqs.q: A flywheel rotating at 1500 revolutions per minute is brought to rest with uniform angular deceleration in 20 s. Through what angular displacement does it turn while stopping? (1 revolution = 2π rad.)
mcqs.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
mcqs.working: ω_i = 1500 rev min⁻¹ × 2π rad/rev ÷ 60 s min⁻¹ = 157.1 rad s⁻¹; ω_f = 0. Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t = (157.1 rad s⁻¹/2)(20 s) = 1571 rad ≈ 1.57 × 10³ rad. (Check: α = −157.1/20 = −7.85 rad s⁻²; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² = 3142 − 1571 = 1571 rad.)
rationales: A student who treats the angular speed as constant uses Δθ = ω_i t = 157 × 20 = 3.14 × 10³ rad. The flywheel slows uniformly, so its average angular speed is half the initial value.
A student who uses 1500 rev min⁻¹ as if it were 1500 rad s⁻¹ gets (1500/2) × 20 = 1.50 × 10⁴ rad. The rate must first be converted: 1500 × 2π/60 = 157 rad s⁻¹.

A student who takes the deceleration as positive uses Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² with α = +7.85 rad s⁻², getting 3142 + 1571 = 4.71 × 10³ rad. For a slowing wheel α is negative, which gives 3142 − 1571 = 1.57 × 10³ rad.

mcqs.q: A wheel starts from rest and turns with a uniform angular acceleration of 3.0 rad s⁻². What is its angular speed at the moment it completes 8.0 revolutions?
mcqs.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
mcqs.explain: Δθ = 8.0 × 2π = 50.3 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2 × 3.0 × 50.3 = 302 rad² s⁻², so ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: Δθ = 8.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 50.27 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2(3.0 rad s⁻²)(50.27 rad) = 301.6 rad² s⁻². ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who uses 8.0 revolutions as 8.0 rad gets ω_f = √(2 × 3.0 × 8.0) = 6.93 rad s⁻¹. Each revolution is 2π rad, so Δθ = 50.3 rad.
A student who drops the factor 2 uses ω_f² = αΔθ = 3.0 × 50.3 and gets 12.3 rad s⁻¹. The equation is ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ.

A student who finds the time (t = √(2Δθ/α) = 5.79 s) and then divides the angle by the time gets 50.3/5.79 = 8.68 rad s⁻¹. That is the average angular speed; starting from rest, the final value is twice as large.
Δθ = 8.0 × 2π = 50.3 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2 × 3.0 × 50.3 = 302 rad² s⁻², so ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: A turntable starts from rest and rotates with uniform angular acceleration. During the first 2.0 s it turns through an angle θ. Through what angle does it turn during the next 2.0 s?
options: θ, as equal time intervals give equal angles turned
2θ, as its angular speed at the end has doubled
3θ, as the angle turned from rest reaches 4θ after 4.0 s
4θ, as the angle is proportional to t², and t doubles
mcqs.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
mcqs.explain: From rest, Δθ = ½αt², so the angle turned from the start is proportional to t². After 4.0 s it is (4.0/2.0)² × θ = 4θ. The angle turned in the second interval is 4θ − θ = 3θ.
mcqs.working: From rest with uniform α: θ(t) = ½αt². θ(2.0 s) = 2α = θ; θ(4.0 s) = 8α = 4θ. Angle turned between 2.0 s and 4.0 s = 4θ − θ = 3θ.
rationales: A student who treats the angular speed as constant picks this. The turntable is accelerating, so it turns faster in the second interval and covers a larger angle.
A student who scales by the final angular speed of each interval picks this. The angle depends on the AVERAGE angular speed in each interval: ½ω₁ in the first and 1½ω₁ in the second, a ratio of 3.
From rest, Δθ = ½αt², so the angle turned from the start is proportional to t². After 4.0 s it is (4.0/2.0)² × θ = 4θ. The angle turned in the second interval is 4θ − θ = 3θ.
A student who confuses the angle turned from the start with the angle turned in the interval picks this. 4θ is the angular position after 4.0 s; θ of that was turned in the first 2.0 s, leaving 3θ.

mcqs.q: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disc have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. Which has the greater moment of inertia about this axis?
options: Neither, because bodies of equal mass have equal moments of inertia.
The hoop, as all its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis.
The disc, since its mass is spread out over its whole area.
Whichever of the two is rotating at the greater angular speed.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the moment of inertia I depends on the distribution of mass of an extended body about an axis of rotation
mcqs.explain: Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. All of the hoop's mass is at distance R (I = MR²); much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis (I = ½MR²).
rationales: A student who treats moment of inertia as the same thing as mass picks this. Moment of inertia depends on the distribution of mass about the axis, not just the amount.
Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. All of the hoop's mass is at distance R (I = MR²); much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis (I = ½MR²).

A student who equates 'spread out' with 'covering more area' picks this. What matters is distance from the axis: the disc has much of its mass close to the centre, so its moment of inertia is smaller.
A student who thinks moment of inertia depends on how fast a body spins picks this. For a rigid body about a given axis, I depends only on the mass distribution.

mcqs.q: A uniform rod of mass M and length L can rotate either about an axis through its centre (I = ML²/12) or about an axis through one end (I = ML²/3), both perpendicular to the rod. The same resultant torque acts in each case. What is the ratio (angular acceleration about the centre)/(angular acceleration about the end)?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the moment of inertia I depends on the distribution of mass of an extended body about an axis of rotation
mcqs.explain: α = τ/I and τ is the same, so α_centre/α_end = I_end/I_centre = (ML²/3)/(ML²/12) = 4.00. Rotating about the centre puts the mass closer to the axis, so I is smaller and α larger.
mcqs.working: α = τ/I; same τ, so α_centre/α_end = I_end/I_centre = (ML²/3)/(ML²/12) = 12/3 = 4.00.
rationales: A student who takes I proportional to distance rather than distance squared argues that the mass is on average L/4 from a central axis and L/2 from an end axis, giving a ratio of 2. Because I depends on r², the ratio is 2² = 4.
A student who thinks a larger moment of inertia gives a larger angular acceleration writes α ∝ I and gets (1/12)/(1/3) = 0.25. In fact α = τ/I, so the body with the smaller I has the larger α.
A student who thinks moment of inertia depends only on mass concludes that the same rod has the same I about any axis. The formulas show I about the end is four times I about the centre.
α = τ/I and τ is the same, so α_centre/α_end = I_end/I_centre = (ML²/3)/(ML²/12) = 4.00. Rotating about the centre puts the mass closer to the axis, so I is smaller and α larger.

mcqs.q: A light rod of length 0.80 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it through its midpoint. Small masses are fixed to the rod: 0.50 kg at end A, 0.20 kg at 0.20 m from end A, and 0.30 kg at end B. The centre of mass of the system is 0.12 m from the axis. What is the moment of inertia of the system about the axis?
mcqs.specStatementText: the moment of inertia for a system of point masses as given by I = Σmr²
mcqs.explain: Distances from the axis are 0.40 m, 0.20 m and 0.40 m. I = Σmr² = 0.50(0.40)² + 0.20(0.20)² + 0.30(0.40)² = 0.080 + 0.008 + 0.048 = 0.136 kg m². The centre-of-mass position is not needed.
mcqs.working: Distances from the axis at the midpoint: A at 0.40 m, the 0.20 kg mass at 0.40 − 0.20 = 0.20 m, B at 0.40 m. I = Σmr² = (0.50 kg)(0.40 m)² + (0.20 kg)(0.20 m)² + (0.30 kg)(0.40 m)² = 0.080 + 0.008 + 0.048 = 0.136 kg m² = 1.4 × 10⁻¹ kg m².
rationales: A student who does not square the distances gets 0.50(0.40) + 0.20(0.20) + 0.30(0.40) = 0.360. That quantity has unit kg m, not kg m²; each distance must be squared.

A student who measures distances from end A gets 0.50(0)² + 0.20(0.20)² + 0.30(0.80)² = 0.200 kg m². That is the moment of inertia about an axis through A; here the axis is at the midpoint, so r = 0.40, 0.20 and 0.40 m.
Distances from the axis are 0.40 m, 0.20 m and 0.40 m. I = Σmr² = 0.50(0.40)² + 0.20(0.20)² + 0.30(0.40)² = 0.080 + 0.008 + 0.048 = 0.136 kg m². The centre-of-mass position is not needed.
A student who places all 1.0 kg at the centre of mass gets 1.0 × (0.12)² = 0.0144 kg m². The centre-of-mass model applies to linear motion; for rotation each mass contributes mr² at its own distance.

mcqs.q: A system of small masses rotates about a fixed axis. Which single change doubles its moment of inertia about that axis?
options: Doubling each mass, with all distances kept unchanged
Doubling each distance from the axis, with all masses unchanged
Doubling the angular speed at which the system is rotating
Adding a mass equal to the total mass, placed on the axis
mcqs.specStatementText: the moment of inertia for a system of point masses as given by I = Σmr²
mcqs.explain: I = Σmr². Doubling every m with every r unchanged doubles every term, so I doubles.
rationales: I = Σmr². Doubling every m with every r unchanged doubles every term, so I doubles.
A student who thinks I is proportional to r picks this. Because I = Σmr², doubling every distance multiplies I by 2² = 4.
A student who thinks moment of inertia depends on how fast the body spins picks this. I depends only on the masses and their distances from the axis; doubling ω doubles L, not I.
A student who treats moment of inertia as mass alone picks this. A mass on the axis has r = 0, so it adds nothing to Σmr²; I is unchanged.

mcqs.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² is driven by a belt that exerts a tangential force of 40 N on its rim, 0.30 m from the axis. A frictional torque of 2.0 N m acts at the bearing, opposing the rotation. What is the angular acceleration of the flywheel?
mcqs.specStatementText: Newton’s second law for rotation as given by τ = Iα where τ is the average torque
mcqs.explain: Driving torque = Fr = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m. The friction torque has the opposite sense, so the resultant torque is 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m, and α = τ/I = 10/0.50 = 20 rad s⁻².
mcqs.working: Driving torque τ₁ = Fr = (40 N)(0.30 m) = 12 N m. Friction torque 2.0 N m in the opposite sense. Resultant τ = 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m. α = τ/I = (10 N m)/(0.50 kg m²) = 20 rad s⁻².
rationales: A student who uses the driving torque alone gets 12/0.50 = 24 rad s⁻². τ in τ = Iα is the resultant torque, so the 2.0 N m friction torque must be subtracted.
Driving torque = Fr = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m. The friction torque has the opposite sense, so the resultant torque is 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m, and α = τ/I = 10/0.50 = 20 rad s⁻².
A student who adds the torques regardless of sense gets (12 + 2.0)/0.50 = 28 rad s⁻². The friction torque opposes the rotation, so it reduces the resultant torque.
A student who uses the belt force as if it were a torque gets (40 − 2.0)/0.50 = 76 rad s⁻². The force must be multiplied by its distance from the axis: τ = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m.

mcqs.q: A uniform disc of mass 3.0 kg and radius 0.20 m rotates at 240 revolutions per minute about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. For this axis, I = ½MR². What is the angular momentum of the disc?
mcqs.specStatementText: that an extended body rotating with an angular speed has an angular momentum L as given by L = Iω
rationales: A student who uses the point-mass formula I = MR² for the disc gets I = 0.12 kg m² and L = 3.02 kg m² s⁻¹. Much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis than R; the given formula is I = ½MR².
A student who uses 240 rev min⁻¹ as if it were 240 rad s⁻¹ gets 0.060 × 240 = 14.4. Convert first: ω = 240 × 2π/60 = 25.1 rad s⁻¹.
A student who does not square the radius gets I = ½ × 3.0 × 0.20 = 0.30 and L = 0.30 × 25.1 = 7.54. The formula is I = ½MR², so R must be squared.

mcqs.q: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis. Its angular momentum about that axis is determined by which quantities?
options: Its mass and angular speed, however the mass is arranged
Its mass and the linear speed of its centre of mass
The resultant torque that is acting on it at that instant
Its moment of inertia about that axis and its angular speed
mcqs.specStatementText: that an extended body rotating with an angular speed has an angular momentum L as given by L = Iω
mcqs.explain: L = Iω. The moment of inertia carries the information about the mass and how it is distributed about the axis; the angular speed says how fast the body turns.
rationales: A student who treats moment of inertia as mass alone picks this. Two bodies of the same mass spinning at the same rate have different angular momenta if their mass is at different distances from the axis.
A student who confuses angular momentum with linear momentum mv picks this. A wheel spinning on a fixed axle has a stationary centre of mass but a non-zero angular momentum Iω.
A student who links the amount of rotation to the torque currently acting picks this. Torque sets the RATE of change of angular momentum; a freely spinning body with no torque still has L = Iω.
L = Iω. The moment of inertia carries the information about the mass and how it is distributed about the axis; the angular speed says how fast the body turns.

mcqs.q: A turntable of moment of inertia 0.020 kg m² rotates freely at 3.0 rad s⁻¹ on a frictionless bearing. A disc of moment of inertia 0.010 kg m², not rotating, is dropped onto it so that both share the same axis. Friction between them soon makes them rotate together. What is their common angular speed?
mcqs.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
mcqs.explain: No external torque acts about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.020 × 3.0 = (0.020 + 0.010)ω, giving ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: No external torque about the axis: L conserved. I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂ = (I₁ + I₂)ω → (0.020)(3.0) + (0.010)(0) = (0.030)ω → ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
rationales: No external torque acts about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.020 × 3.0 = (0.020 + 0.010)ω, giving ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
A student who thinks the angular speed is conserved when there is no external torque picks this. The moment of inertia has increased, so to keep Iω constant the angular speed must fall.
A student who averages the two angular speeds, (3.0 + 0)/2, gets 1.5 rad s⁻¹. The speeds must be weighted by the moments of inertia: the turntable has twice the disc's I.
A student who conserves kinetic energy, ½(0.020)(3.0)² = ½(0.030)ω², gets 2.4 rad s⁻¹. Friction between the discs dissipates energy, so kinetic energy is not conserved; angular momentum is.

mcqs.q: A student sits on a stool that rotates freely about a vertical axis. She holds a 2.5 kg mass in each hand at 0.80 m from the axis and rotates at 2.0 rad s⁻¹. She then pulls both masses in to 0.20 m from the axis. Take the moment of inertia of the student and stool, without the masses, as a constant 2.0 kg m², and treat the masses as point masses. What is her new angular speed?
mcqs.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
mcqs.explain: I_i = 2.0 + 2 × 2.5 × 0.80² = 5.2 kg m²; I_f = 2.0 + 2 × 2.5 × 0.20² = 2.2 kg m². With no external torque, I_iω_i = I_fω_f, so ω_f = 5.2 × 2.0/2.2 = 4.7 rad s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: I_i = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.80 m)² = 2.0 + 3.2 = 5.2 kg m². I_f = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.20 m)² = 2.0 + 0.20 = 2.2 kg m². No external torque about the axis: I_iω_i = I_fω_f → ω_f = (5.2)(2.0)/2.2 = 4.7 rad s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who does not square the distances gets I_i = 2.0 + 5.0 × 0.80 = 6.0 and I_f = 2.0 + 5.0 × 0.20 = 3.0, so ω_f = 4.0 rad s⁻¹. Each mass contributes mr².
I_i = 2.0 + 2 × 2.5 × 0.80² = 5.2 kg m²; I_f = 2.0 + 2 × 2.5 × 0.20² = 2.2 kg m². With no external torque, I_iω_i = I_fω_f, so ω_f = 5.2 × 2.0/2.2 = 4.7 rad s⁻¹.
A student who conserves kinetic energy, ½I_iω_i² = ½I_fω_f², gets 3.1 rad s⁻¹. The student does work pulling the masses in, so kinetic energy increases; the conserved quantity is angular momentum.
A student who thinks angular speed stays constant without an external torque picks this. The moment of inertia has fallen from 5.2 to 2.2 kg m², so ω must rise to keep Iω constant.

mcqs.q: A diver leaves a springboard rotating slowly with her body straight. In the air she pulls into a tight tuck and rotates much faster. Air resistance is negligible. Why does her angular speed increase?
options: Her moment of inertia decreases while her angular momentum stays constant.
Pulling in her limbs exerts an external torque on her, which speeds her up.
Her weight exerts a torque about her centre of mass as she falls.
Her angular momentum increases as she falls and her speed increases.
mcqs.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
mcqs.explain: In the air no external torque acts about her centre of mass, so her angular momentum Iω is constant. Tucking brings mass closer to the axis, reducing I, so ω increases.
rationales: In the air no external torque acts about her centre of mass, so her angular momentum Iω is constant. Tucking brings mass closer to the axis, reducing I, so ω increases.

A student who thinks any increase in angular speed needs an external torque picks this. The forces that pull her limbs in are internal; they cannot change her total angular momentum. The spin rate rises because I falls.

A student who links the fall to the faster spin picks this. Her weight acts at her centre of mass, so it has no torque about that point; it accelerates her centre of mass downward but does not change her spin.

A student who confuses angular momentum with linear momentum picks this. Her linear momentum increases as she falls, but her angular momentum about her centre of mass is constant because no torque acts about it.

mcqs.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² rotates counter-clockwise at 12 rad s⁻¹. A torque acts on it for 2.0 s, after which the wheel rotates clockwise at 4.0 rad s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the average torque on the wheel?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
mcqs.explain: Taking counter-clockwise as positive, ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = 0.50 × (−4.0 − 12) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0, a torque of 4.0 N m in the clockwise sense.
mcqs.working: Take counter-clockwise as positive: ω_i = +12 rad s⁻¹, ω_f = −4.0 rad s⁻¹. ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = (0.50 kg m²)(−16 rad s⁻¹) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0 = −4.0 N m, i.e. 4.0 N m clockwise.
rationales: A student who takes the change in angular speed as the larger value minus the smaller gets 0.50 × (12 − 4.0)/2.0 = 2.0 N m. The wheel reverses: with counter-clockwise positive, Δω = (−4.0) − (+12) = −16 rad s⁻¹, so the average torque has magnitude 0.50 × 16/2.0 = 4.0 N m.

A student who takes the change in angular momentum to be the final angular momentum uses 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 N m s and gets 1.0 N m. The initial angular momentum must be subtracted: ΔL = L_final − L_initial.
Taking counter-clockwise as positive, ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = 0.50 × (−4.0 − 12) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0, a torque of 4.0 N m in the clockwise sense.
A student who equates the torque with the angular impulse gives 0.50 × 16 = 8.0 as the torque. 8.0 N m s is the angular impulse; dividing by the 2.0 s gives the average torque, 4.0 N m.

mcqs.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.25 kg m² rotates counter-clockwise at 40 rad s⁻¹. A clockwise torque is then applied. A graph of the magnitude of this torque against time rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 4.0 N m at t = 0.50 s, stays at 4.0 N m until t = 1.50 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 2.0 s. No other torque acts. What is the angular speed of the wheel at t = 2.0 s?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
mcqs.explain: Angular impulse = area under the graph = ½(0.50)(4.0) + (1.0)(4.0) + ½(0.50)(4.0) = 6.0 N m s, clockwise. Initial L = 0.25 × 40 = 10 kg m² s⁻¹ counter-clockwise, so final L = 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 and ω = 4.0/0.25 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹, still counter-clockwise.
mcqs.working: Angular impulse = area under τ–t graph = ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) + (1.00 s)(4.0 N m) + ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) = 1.0 + 4.0 + 1.0 = 6.0 N m s (clockwise). Take counter-clockwise as positive: L_i = (0.25)(40) = 10 kg m² s⁻¹; L_f = 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 kg m² s⁻¹; ω_f = 4.0/0.25 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹, counter-clockwise.
rationales: A student who ignores the sense of the torque adds the angular impulse: (10 + 6.0)/0.25 = 64.0 rad s⁻¹. The torque is clockwise and the wheel turns counter-clockwise, so the torque reduces the angular momentum.
A student who takes the angular impulse as the final angular momentum gets 6.0/0.25 = 24.0 rad s⁻¹. 24.0 rad s⁻¹ is the CHANGE in angular speed; the final value is 40 − 24 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹.

A student who multiplies the peak torque by the whole time uses 4.0 × 2.0 = 8.0 N m s and gets (10 − 8.0)/0.25 = 8.00 rad s⁻¹. The average torque is less than the peak; the angular impulse is the area under the graph, 6.0 N m s.

Angular impulse = area under the graph = ½(0.50)(4.0) + (1.0)(4.0) + ½(0.50)(4.0) = 6.0 N m s, clockwise. Initial L = 0.25 × 40 = 10 kg m² s⁻¹ counter-clockwise, so final L = 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 and ω = 4.0/0.25 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹, still counter-clockwise.

mcqs.q: A solid cylinder of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope, descending a vertical height of 0.90 m. For the cylinder, I = ½MR². Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and ignore energy dissipation. What is the speed of its centre of mass at the bottom of the slope?
mcqs.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
mcqs.explain: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R and I = ½MR², so Mgh = ½Mv² + ¼Mv² = ¾Mv². v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 9.8 × 0.90/3) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: E_p lost = Mgh = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(0.90 m) = 17.64 J. Rolling without slipping: ω = v/R. E_k = ½Mv² + ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¾Mv² = 1.5v² (in J, v in m s⁻¹). 1.5v² = 17.64 → v² = 11.76 → v = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who ignores rotational kinetic energy uses Mgh = ½Mv² and gets v = √(2gh) = 4.2 m s⁻¹. That is the speed of a body sliding without friction; a rolling cylinder puts a third of its kinetic energy into rotation.
Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R and I = ½MR², so Mgh = ½Mv² + ¼Mv² = ¾Mv². v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 9.8 × 0.90/3) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
A student who writes rotational kinetic energy as Iω² (no ½) gets Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Mv², so v = √(gh) = 3.0 m s⁻¹. Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω² = ¼Mv² here.
A student who does not square R in I = ½MR² gets I = 0.10 and ½Iω² = 5v², so 17.64 = v² + 5v² and v = 1.7 m s⁻¹. With R squared, I = 0.010 kg m² and ½Iω² = 0.50v².

mcqs.q: A skater spinning on ice with negligible friction pulls her arms in towards her body and spins faster. How do her angular momentum L and her rotational kinetic energy E_k change?
options: L is unchanged; E_k is unchanged, since no external work is done.
L increases, because her mass is the same and she spins faster; E_k increases.
L is unchanged; E_k increases, as she does work pulling her arms in.
L increases, as pulling her arms in exerts a torque on her; E_k increases.
mcqs.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
mcqs.explain: No external torque acts, so L = Iω is constant. E_k = L²/2I, and I decreases, so E_k increases. The extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling her arms inward.
rationales: A student who assumes kinetic energy is conserved whenever angular momentum is picks this. E_k = L²/2I: with L fixed and I smaller, E_k must rise. Internal forces (her muscles) do the work.
A student who thinks the moment of inertia depends only on mass assumes I is unchanged, so faster spin means more L. Pulling her arms in reduces I; L = Iω stays constant.
No external torque acts, so L = Iω is constant. E_k = L²/2I, and I decreases, so E_k increases. The extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling her arms inward.
A student who thinks any spin-up needs an external torque picks this. The forces pulling her arms in are internal and cannot change her total angular momentum; ω rises because I falls.

mcqs.q: A thin hoop of mass 3.0 kg (I = MR²) and a solid cylinder of mass 1.0 kg (I = ½MR²), with equal radii, are released together from rest at the top of the same slope. Both roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
options: The cylinder, as a smaller fraction of its E_k is rotational.
The hoop, because it is the heavier and so it accelerates faster.
They arrive together, as the acceleration does not depend on mass.
The hoop, because its larger moment of inertia keeps it rolling faster.
mcqs.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
mcqs.explain: For rolling without slipping, E_k = ½Mv²(1 + I/MR²). The cylinder (I/MR² = ½) has v² = 4gh/3 at each height; the hoop (I/MR² = 1) has v² = gh. The cylinder is faster at every point and arrives first; the masses cancel.
rationales: For rolling without slipping, E_k = ½Mv²(1 + I/MR²). The cylinder (I/MR² = ½) has v² = 4gh/3 at each height; the hoop (I/MR² = 1) has v² = gh. The cylinder is faster at every point and arrives first; the masses cancel.
A student who believes heavier objects move down faster picks this. A larger weight comes with a proportionally larger inertia, so mass cancels; only the mass distribution (I/MR²) matters.
A student who over-generalises free fall picks this. The mass does cancel, but the shapes differ: the hoop puts half its kinetic energy into rotation, the cylinder only a third.
A student who reads 'inertia' as a tendency to keep going faster picks this. A larger I/MR² means more of the lost E_p goes into rotation, so the hoop gains LESS speed.

mcqs.q: A thin hoop (I = MR²) and a uniform solid disc (I = ½MR²) have the same mass M and the same radius R. Each is mounted on a frictionless axle through its centre, perpendicular to its plane, and is initially at rest. The same constant resultant torque τ is then applied to each. Which statement correctly compares their subsequent motion?
options: The hoop has twice the angular acceleration of the disc, because its larger moment of inertia responds more to the torque.
After equal times the disc is turning faster, because its angular acceleration is twice that of the hoop.
The two angular accelerations are equal, because the bodies have equal mass and the same torque acts on each.
Each body turns at a constant angular speed, and the two speeds are equal because the torques are equal.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newton’s second law for rotation as given by τ = Iα where τ is the average torque
mcqs.explain: From τ = Iα, α = τ/I. The disc's moment of inertia is half the hoop's, so for the same torque its angular acceleration is twice as large: α_disc = 2τ/MR², α_hoop = τ/MR². Starting from rest, ω = αt, so after any equal time the disc has the greater angular speed.
rationales: A student who treats moment of inertia as a measure of how strongly a body responds to a torque picks this. Moment of inertia is resistance to angular acceleration: α = τ/I, so the larger I of the hoop gives it the smaller angular acceleration, half that of the disc.

From τ = Iα, α = τ/I. The disc's moment of inertia is half the hoop's, so for the same torque its angular acceleration is twice as large: α_disc = 2τ/MR², α_hoop = τ/MR². Starting from rest, ω = αt, so after any equal time the disc has the greater angular speed.

A student who takes moment of inertia to be just the rotational name for mass picks this. Equal masses do not give equal moments of inertia: I depends on how the mass is distributed about the axis, and the hoop's mass is all at radius R, giving it twice the disc's I and half its angular acceleration.

A student who thinks a steady torque produces a steady angular speed picks this. A resultant torque produces angular acceleration, not a fixed angular speed: while τ acts, each body's angular speed keeps increasing, at a rate α = τ/I that is different for the two bodies.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Physics (guide first assessment 2025, updated November 2023); topic A.4 Rigid body mechanics
topicGuidance: The vector nature of torque and angular momentum need not be addressed, but the sense (clockwise or counter-clockwise) of a torque should be included.

A calculation of the centre of mass of bodies is not required; there should be an understanding that when considering linear motion, the mass of an extended body may be taken as concentrated at the centre of mass.
The equation for the moment of inertia of a specific mass distribution will be provided when necessary.
Simultaneous rotational and translational motion will be restricted to rolling without slipping.
Angular speed will be used rather than angular velocity as a formal vector treatment.
The term angular velocity will be used although a formal vector treatment is not required.
Situations should involve change of moment of inertia in extended bodies and coupled pairs of bodies.

scopeNotes.statement: The vector nature of torque and angular momentum need not be addressed, but the sense (clockwise or counter-clockwise) of a torque should be included.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Torque is treated as a magnitude with a sense (clockwise or counter-clockwise), and the sense is used in every equilibrium and resultant-torque item. No item uses the vector (cross) product or asks for the direction of a torque vector along the axis.

scopeNotes.statement: A calculation of the centre of mass of bodies is not required; there should be an understanding that when considering linear motion, the mass of an extended body may be taken as concentrated at the centre of mass.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks the student to locate a centre of mass. Where the position of a centre of mass is needed it is given in the stem (for example, the weight of a uniform plank acts at its midpoint).

scopeNotes.statement: A calculation of the centre of mass of bodies is not required; there should be an understanding that when considering linear motion, the mass of an extended body may be taken as concentrated at the centre of mass.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Centre-of-mass ideas are used only as the guidance intends: the linear motion of an extended body is that of its whole mass concentrated at the centre of mass. The position of the centre of mass is never calculated.

scopeNotes.statement: Simultaneous rotational and translational motion will be restricted to rolling without slipping.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The rolling item uses only the no-slip condition v = ωr; no item treats a wheel that slips or skids.

scopeNotes.statement: Angular speed will be used rather than angular velocity as a formal vector treatment.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Angular speed ω is used in all calculations and angular velocity appears only as a descriptive term; no item treats angular velocity as a vector with a direction along the axis.

scopeNotes.statement: The equation for the moment of inertia of a specific mass distribution will be provided when necessary.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every moment-of-inertia formula for an extended body (rod, disc, cylinder, hoop) is stated in the stem. Students are expected to know only I = Σmr² for point masses; no formula for a continuous body has to be recalled or derived.

scopeNotes.statement: The vector nature of torque and angular momentum need not be addressed, but the sense (clockwise or counter-clockwise) of a torque should be included.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Angular momentum is treated as the scalar Iω about a fixed axis, with a sense of rotation where a reversal matters. No item assigns angular momentum a vector direction or uses the right-hand rule.

scopeNotes.statement: Simultaneous rotational and translational motion will be restricted to rolling without slipping.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only items that analyse rotation and translation together (q07, q24, q26) involve bodies rolling without slipping, with v = ωR. No item involves skidding, sliding with spin or rolling with slipping: in q05 the free bar's centre of mass stays at rest, and q21 treats only the diver's rotation, not her flight path.

scopeNotes.statement: Situations should involve change of moment of inertia in extended bodies and coupled pairs of bodies.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Change of moment of inertia of an extended body is tested in q20 (a student on a stool pulls in two masses) and q21 (a diver pulls into a tuck), and again in q25 on A.4.12 (a skater pulls in her arms). A coupled pair of bodies is tested in q19 (a disc dropped onto a rotating turntable).
